research_text:
## Research brief

### 1. API and finding

`javax.crypto.Mac` implements message-authentication-code algorithms for checking the integrity of stored or transmitted information using a shared secret key. HMAC is a MAC construction based on a cryptographic hash function. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Mac.html))

For this finding, the relevant value is the **algorithm-name argument to `Mac.getInstance`**. The reported value, `HmacSHA1`, names HMAC using SHA-1; it is not the key or the computed MAC. Java SE documents `HmacSHA1` as a supported standard algorithm, while the supplied CrySL rule excludes that exact name. API availability and compliance with this particular rule are therefore different questions. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Mac.html))

Oracle API source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Mac.html

### 2. Documented usage and remediation guidance

The API documents selecting an algorithm with `getInstance`, initializing the object with an appropriate key and, where required, parameters, then processing data with `update` and/or `doFinal`. `doFinal` returns or writes the result and resets the object to its initialized state; reusing it with a different key requires reinitialization. An output buffer must have room for the complete result. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Mac.html))

For HMAC, RFC 2104 identifies random or cryptographically pseudorandom keys, secure key exchange, key refresh, and protection of key secrecy as important to safe use. ([datatracker.ietf.org](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc2104/))  
RFC source: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc2104/

**The `Mac` API documentation does not prescribe a universal remediation for `HmacSHA1`.** It documents both `HmacSHA1` and `HmacSHA256`. Separately, NIST announced a transition away from SHA-1 for applying cryptographic protection by December 31, 2030. The rule permits `HmacSHA256`, but the appropriate choice depends on the applicable protocol and policy; the rule’s password-based names describe different schemes, not necessarily interchangeable HMAC replacements. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Mac.html))

NIST source: https://csrc.nist.gov/news/2022/nist-transitioning-away-from-sha-1-for-all-apps

### 3. Compatibility and migration

- **Tags and formats:** HMAC’s underlying hash is part of its definition. Changing it changes the calculation; the full SHA-1 and SHA-256 hash outputs are 160 and 256 bits respectively. Existing persisted tags and wire formats must therefore be considered; truncation, if any, is protocol-specific. This is an inference from the HMAC definition, not a migration procedure specified by `Mac`. ([datatracker.ietf.org](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc2104/))
- **Platform and provider support:** Java SE 7 documents both `HmacSHA1` and `HmacSHA256` as required. Java SE 26 also requires both and lists `PBEWithHmacSHA256`; other algorithms and explicitly selected providers require separate support checks. A named or supplied provider may lack the requested implementation. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/7/docs/api/javax/crypto/Mac.html?trk=article-ssr-frontend-pulse_little-text-block&utm_source=openai))
- **Migration path:** The `Mac` documentation does not define a persisted-format or wire-protocol migration path, negotiation mechanism, or automatic conversion of old tags. NIST notes that SHA-1 may still be needed to handle information protected before its transition date, but does not give a Java-specific migration procedure there. ([csrc.nist.gov](https://csrc.nist.gov/news/2022/nist-transitioning-away-from-sha-1-for-all-apps))

### 4. Exact rule source and limits

The supplied rule file declares `SPEC javax.crypto.Mac`. Its factory-event matching clause and algorithm constraint are reproduced verbatim below. The file declares `algorithm` as `java.lang.String`. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/Mac.crysl))

```text
g1: getInstance(algorithm);
g2: getInstance(algorithm, _);
Get := g1 | g2;
```

```text
algorithm in {"HmacSHA256", "HmacSHA384", "HmacSHA512", "HmacPBESHA1", "PBEWithHmacSHA1", "PBEWithHmacSHA224", "PBEWithHmacSHA256", "PBEWithHmacSHA384", "PBEWithHmacSHA512"};
```

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/Mac.crysl

- The relevant method name is **`getInstance`**, scoped by the file’s `SPEC` declaration to `javax.crypto.Mac`. The two event clauses specify **one or two arguments**; the second argument in the latter is written `_`. They are factory calls, rather than instance-receiver calls.
- The file also names `init`, `update`, and `doFinal` events in its lifecycle specification, but the quoted algorithm constraint concerns the `algorithm` object used in the factory events. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/Mac.crysl))
- **A method merely sharing the name is not specified as a name-only match:** the file declares the governed `Mac` type. However, the file itself does not explain a detector’s method-resolution implementation, so it cannot establish whether a particular detector might nevertheless report an unrelated same-named method.
- The detector message includes six `HMAC-...` or `HMAC/...` spellings that are **not present** in the retrieved rule’s nine-name constraint. The file alone does not explain that discrepancy.
- The URL points to a mutable branch. The supplied SHA-256 was **not independently verified** against the retrieved bytes; consequently, an exact match to the originally reported rule version remains unresolved.
